title: The Epistle to the Brothers of Mont-Dieu

blocks.s: In the letter to the Brothers of Mont-Dieu, Bernard treats at length the progress of the soul toward God in the contemplative life. Among his teachings there: the soul has a certain natural likeness to God that none loses; there is a closer likeness by which the soul strives to imitate the Creator's greatness of virtue and steadfastness; and beyond this is a likeness so properly the soul's own that it is called not likeness but unity of spirit (unitas spiritus), when a person becomes one with God — not only by identity of will, but by a certain unity of virtue beyond all willing otherwise. This unity of spirit is called such not only because the Holy Spirit effects it, or because he joins the human spirit to himself, but because this unity itself is the Holy Spirit, who is the Love, the Unity, the Sweetness, the Kiss, and the Embrace of the Father and the Son.

In this unity the blessed conscience finds itself somehow in the middle of the embrace and kiss of Father and Son, and in an ineffable and inconceivable manner is made the homo Dei, not God, but what God is by nature the person becomes by grace. The Holy Spirit is the all-powerful artificer who creates in the human being a good will toward God, who makes God propitious toward the human being, who forms affection, gives virtue, prospers action, orders all things mightily and disposes all things sweetly (cf. Wisd. 8:1), and who himself teaches how to find, to hold, and to enjoy.
